## Sample kind
Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.

- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
# The Department of Small Repairs

On the first Saturday of every month, the city opened a room beneath the railway station where you could bring one broken thing. The rules were printed on a sheet of paper taped to the door: NO PHONES. NO MICROWAVES. YOU MUST STAY WITH YOUR OBJECT. That last rule was underlined twice. People assumed it meant there had been trouble with unclaimed toasters, but the volunteers had put it there because otherwise everyone went for coffee, and the room was too quiet.

Marta first came in November with a wooden duck. It was the kind that followed a child on a string, its wheels turning two flat orange feet that slapped the floor. One foot had split down the middle. Her son had graduated from university the previous summer and was now living in a city so flat, he said, that when you lost a dog you could watch it run away for three days. She had been saving that joke to tell someone in person.

“What kind of wood is it?” asked the man at the first table.

“I don’t know.”

“That’s all right. Neither do I.”

His name was Len. He took the duck apart and placed the pieces in a muffin tin. Beside them, in a compartment of its own, he placed a screw so small Marta could only see it when it caught the light. Then he asked her to hold the broken foot while he drew around it on a scrap of wood.

Above them a train came in. The ceiling trembled. At the next table a girl in a school uniform was learning to sew a button onto her own coat. She had buttoned it wrong on purpose so no one could see the gap. A woman with a suitcase sat with one stockinged foot resting on the other while a volunteer glued the sole of her shoe. It was an ordinary room, apart from the unusual number of people sitting still while something they needed was in pieces.

The new foot was paler than the old one. Len offered to paint it, but Marta said she liked being able to tell which one it was. He set the duck on the floor and drew it toward him. It made three good slaps, then fell on its side.

“I put the wheels on backward,” he said.

They laughed, although it wasn’t much of a joke. Then Marta told him the one about the dog.

By February she was a volunteer. Her first repair was a zipper on a cushion cover. She spent forty minutes coaxing the slider back onto the track, only for the cushion’s owner to turn the cover right side out and reveal a large burn in the shape of an iron.

“Did you want us to do something about that, too?” Marta asked.

“No,” the woman said. “My sister did that.”

She said it with such satisfaction that Marta didn’t ask another question.

Some things couldn’t be fixed. A boy brought in a snow globe with a crack at the base. Someone had already tried to seal it with candle wax. By the time he arrived, the little village inside stood dry beneath a blue sky, its snow gathered in an untidy drift along one wall. Len explained that even if they sealed the crack, he wasn’t sure how they’d get the liquid back in. The boy considered this.

“Can you make it snow one more time?”

Len turned the globe upside down and tapped the glass. A few flakes came loose. They fell much faster than snow should, but the boy watched until the last one landed.

In April, a council employee came downstairs carrying a clipboard. The station was being renovated. The room was needed for electrical equipment. She had been told, she said, that they offered a drop-off service.

“No,” Marta said, pointing at the rules.

The employee read the sheet. “Why can’t people drop things off?”

Marta looked around. Len was holding a lamp while its owner, an elderly man in a beautifully ironed shirt, tried to thread the cord through the base. Every time the cord appeared, the man reached for it too quickly and knocked it back inside. At last Len set down the lamp, took two pairs of tweezers from a drawer, and handed him one.

“Sometimes we need both of you,” Marta said.

They were given until June. On the last Saturday, people kept arriving with things that weren’t broken. The girl who had learned to sew on a button brought a cake in a tin with a perfectly sound hinge. The man with the lamp brought a photograph of it switched on. Someone brought a folding chair, circled the room twice looking for a place to put it, then unfolded it and sat down.

Marta had brought the duck. Her son was coming home the following week, and she had decided to give it to him, though she suspected he would say, quite reasonably, that he had nowhere to put it. She set it on Len’s table. He ran a thumb over the pale foot. It was already acquiring the grayish look of the older one.

“Needs a bit of oil,” he said.

“Does it?”

“No. I just thought we could do it anyway.”

So they did. At five they packed the muffin tins and took the sign off the door. Upstairs, the woman with the suitcase was waiting in the station café. She had asked the manager if they could use the back tables next month, and he’d said yes, provided nobody plugged anything in.

“What will we do about lamps?” Len asked.

“Bring one and find out,” she said.

The floor in the café was tiled, so Marta put the duck down to see how it sounded there. Louder, it turned out. It slapped its way past a man buttering a scone and stopped under the chair of a little girl. Marta crouched to retrieve it, but the girl had already slipped down from her seat. She picked up the string and looked at Marta.

“Can I take it back the other way?”

Marta moved her chair out of the way.
---

Condition: MID

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A quiet, gently comic story uses a community repair room to explore care, attention, and the ways people stay connected.

## Grounded reading
The voice is tender and observant, finding emotional weight in practical details: a screw catching the light, a cord slipping back inside a lamp, a duck’s mismatched wooden foot. Its pathos is restrained rather than tragic; people carry loneliness, family distance, and private history into the room, but the story lets those feelings emerge through small acts and understated exchanges. The ending invites the reader to understand repair as something people do together, even when the object—or the original arrangement—cannot be fully restored.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds broken household objects, patient hands, and the rule that people must stay with what they bring. It gives particular attention to companionship built through shared tasks, to accepting visible signs of repair, and to making a place for people even after its official purpose ends. Its humor is mild and affectionate, and its moral emphasis falls on presence rather than efficiency.

## Evidence line
> It was an ordinary room, apart from the unusual number of people sitting still while something they needed was in pieces.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The coherent imagery of repair, waiting, and shared attention makes this a distinctive sample, with those concerns recurring through the objects, dialogue, and resolution.
